I could not resist and performed a quick test with the latest Ventura AirportItlwm release from May 5th from DexterSLamb's fork on my AX210 under macOS Tahoe 26.5.1.

Unfortunately, AirDrop still does not work and awdl0 is still not being created:

ifconfig awdl0

returns:

ifconfig: interface awdl0 does not exist

I also checked:

show State:/Network/Interface/en2/LinkQuality

which currently reports:

LinkQuality : 100

However, I never checked the LinkQuality value with the upstream AirportItlwm build before, so I cannot yet say whether this represents a change introduced by the fork or not.

At least from my initial testing, the fork does not appear to restore AWDL functionality under Tahoe 26.5.1, although additional testing may still be needed.

Many thanks for the suggestion nevertheless — it was definitely worth a try.

If you don’t have the SSDT configured yet, I would first focus on getting Wi-Fi patching working correctly. The SSDT can always be added later as a refinement once everything else is up and running. 😉

I hope you added the correct PCI device path for the Wi-Fi card to DeviceProperties in your config.plist and not to the SSDT. 😊

However, since you are now able to apply the Modern Wi-Fi Root Patch, the Broadcom IOName spoofing seems to be working correctly.

If Wi-Fi still does not load or connect, I would next verify the following:

- AppleVTD is disabled, i.e. DisableIoMapper = true
- the correct AirportItlwm.kext is used and enabled
- the required kext entries under Kernel → Add are present and enabled (AMFIPass.kext, IOSkywalkFamily.kext, IO80211FamilyLegacy.kext and IO80211FamilyLegacy.kext/Contents/PlugIns/AirPortBrcmNIC.kext)
- the required Kernel → Block entries for the com.apple.iokit.IOSkywalkFamily replacement are present and enabled with Strategy = Exclude
- the boot argument -amfipassbeta is active

Also make sure that the SSDT from my package is not reused blindly, because it contains my own PCI/ACPI path and must be adapted to your hardware.

If you are not familiar with ACPI modifications, I would simply skip the SSDT for now. As mentioned before, it is not required to make Wi-Fi work. The SSDT is mainly intended to provide a clean and properly named ACPI device for the Wi-Fi card and to keep the ACPI implementation consistent.

By the way, this status report was originally intended to gather feedback, test results and contributions regarding the current Intel AWDL situation under Tahoe rather than to provide a complete setup guide for the Intel Wi-Fi approach described above. 😄

Contributions from OpenIntelWireless developers, testers and other community members are therefore highly appreciated.

The main goal of this status report is to help move Intel AWDL support under Tahoe forward.

However, never mind — if you run into further issues while setting up the configuration, feel free to post here and I'll try to help where I can.

Your questions might also help others who are trying to set up the Intel Wi-Fi approach described above.

Personally, I do not think Internet Sharing is directly related to the current AWDL issue. Internet Sharing uses the normal Wi-Fi interface, whereas AWDL relies on a separate virtual interface called awdl0.

The more important observation is that awdl0 does not appear to be created at all.

We now have similar reports for AX201, AX210, AX211 and BE200, which suggests that the issue is probably not limited to a specific Intel chipset.

At the moment, this points more towards a common AirportItlwm-issue rather than a chipset-specific problem.

Small AWDL / AirDrop update after debugging of Dexterxxx’s AirportItlwm-Ventura code on AX210 / macOS 26.5.2 (25F84).

Scope of this test first:

All modifications were strictly limited to AWDL / AirDrop debugging only.

No unrelated parts of AirportItlwm were intentionally changed. In particular, I did not attempt to modify normal Wi-Fi association, scanning, Bluetooth, power management, firmware loading or general driver behaviour.

The only purpose of these debug builds was to understand why awdl0 is not created with the original Dexterxxx Ventura code and why AirDrop / AWDL TX does not become functional even after awdl0 is successfully attached.

Important clarification:

With the original Dexterxxx AirportItlwm-Ventura code, awdl0 does not get created at all on my AX210 / macOS 26.5.2 test setup.

During debugging, I had to remove or bypass several AWDL-related blocking code paths / early-return sections before the AWDL virtual interface could be attached successfully.

After these AWDL-specific blocking sections were removed or bypassed, the situation changed significantly:

- awdl0 is created and active.
- awdl0 is registered as IO80211P2PInterface.
- wifip2pd attaches successfully via IO80211AsyncEventUserClient.
- requestPacketTx() is called for awdl0.
- pendingPackets(0), queueSize(0) and packetSpace(0) report a valid AWDL queue state.
- AirDrop / nearby discovery becomes visible at userland level.

So the first important result is:

The current Dexterxxx AirportItlwm-Ventura code still contains AWDL-related blocks that prevent awdl0 from being loaded in the first place. Once those blocks are removed or bypassed, AWDL interface creation and userland attachment actually work.

However, the remaining problem is the actual AWDL TX dequeue path.

Even with awdl0 loaded correctly, no mbuf is produced from the AWDL TX queue:

- dequeueTxPackets(&request) returns null.
- request.bufs[0] and request.bufs[1] remain null.
- dequeueOutputPacketsWithServiceClass(...) also returns null for all tested service classes.
- AirportItlwm::outputPacket() still only sees primary interface traffic, not real awdl0 frames.

As a last-resort test, I tried a guarded one-shot call to:

    IO80211P2PInterface::outputStart(uint)

from AirportItlwm::requestPacketTx(), only when pendingPackets(0) was greater than zero.

Result: immediate kernel panic.

The panic backtrace shows:

    IO80211VirtualInterface::_outputStartGated()
     -> AirportItlwm::requestPacketTx()
     -> IO80211P2PInterface::initIfnetEparams()
     -> IO80211VirtualInterface::initIfnetEparams()
     -> page fault

The backtrace explicitly contains both:

    com.apple.iokit.IO80211FamilyLegacy(1200.12.2b1)
    com.zxystd.AirportItlwm(2.3.105)

This confirms that outputStart(uint) is not a safe external dequeue/kick path for AWDL/P2P TX from requestPacketTx(). It appears to enter Apple’s private gated P2P / ifnet setup path instead of simply releasing queued AWDL packets.

Current status:

- Original Dexterxxx Ventura code: awdl0 does not load because of AWDL-related blocking code paths.
- Modified AWDL-only debug code: awdl0 loads successfully as IO80211P2PInterface.
- wifip2pd attachment: working.
- AWDL TX request callback: working.
- AWDL queue state: visible.
- AWDL TX dequeue: still blocked.
- outputStart(uint) workaround: unsafe / causes kernel panic.

So the investigation has reached two separate conclusions:

1. There are still AWDL-related code blocks in the current Ventura AirportItlwm path that prevent awdl0 creation and need to be removed or reworked.

2. After awdl0 creation is fixed, the next missing piece is the Apple-private IO80211P2PInterface / IO80211VirtualInterface TX queue handshake. The queued AWDL packets are visible, but the driver still cannot safely dequeue them for transmission.

This is not a usable fix yet, and I will not publish this experimental kext.

Nevertheless, the debug result is important because it shows that AWDL / AirDrop can be brought much further than before once the initial blocking sections are removed. The current hard boundary is no longer awdl0 creation, CoreWLAN registration, wifip2pd attachment, ACPI or IOName spoofing, but the remaining private AWDL/P2P TX queue handshake.

Additional AWDL TX datapath debugging update:

I did some further low-level tracing of the AWDL virtual interface TX path on my AX210 setup.

The main new finding is that the AWDL control plane appears to be alive, but the pending AWDL TX packets are not exposed through the legacy mbuf dequeue paths currently used by AirportItlwm.

Current confirmed state:

awdl0 is created successfully.
attachVirtualInterface() succeeds.
enableVirtualInterface() succeeds.
awdl0 is UP, RUNNING and active.
The interface role is 6.
The AWDL object is confirmed to be an IO80211P2PInterface.
The AWDL interface has a valid ifnet.
ifconfig awdl0 reports options=400<CHANNEL_IO>.

I then traced the TX side more closely.

pendingPackets(0) reports pending AWDL TX packets, and packetSpace(0) changes consistently with that pending count. However, none of the legacy dequeue paths I tested returns any packets.

Tested paths:

dequeueTxPackets(TxPacketRequest *)

The TxPacketRequest structure appears to be accepted and modified by Apple’s code. pkt_cnt is consumed and changed to 0, and reqTx is modified as well. However, all returned packet buffers remain null.

Different reqTx masks

I tested:

0xffffffff
0x0000ffff
0x00000001
0x00000010

All of them are consumed, but no mbuf is returned.

Different packet counts

I tested:

pkt_cnt = 1
pkt_cnt = pendingPackets(Q0)
pkt_cnt = 16

Again, the request is processed, but no packet is returned.

dequeueOutputPacketsWithServiceClass()

I also tested the service-class dequeue path across the known service classes. The method returns successfully, but all heads/tails remain null, and count/byte values stay at 0.

The most interesting new part was the DLT / IOOutputQueue tracing.

A sweep over several DLTs showed that almost all tested DLT output queues are null. However, DLT12 exposes a valid IOOutputQueue.

I then added a passive getter-only trace for that DLT12 queue:

DLT12-PRESENT = yes
DLT12-CAPACITY = 32
DLT12-SIZE = 0

At the same time, pendingPackets(0) still reports pending AWDL packets.

So DLT12 is real and initialized, but it is not where the pending AWDL TX packets are sitting.

This seems to narrow the problem down quite a bit:

AirportItlwm can create and enable an apparently valid AWDL IO80211P2PInterface, and macOS reports awdl0 as active with CHANNEL_IO. But the pending AWDL TX packets are not available through dequeueTxPackets(), not through the service-class dequeue path, and not through the visible DLT12 IOOutputQueue.

Therefore, the remaining missing piece looks less like AWDL interface creation/enablement and more like an unwired or unimplemented CHANNEL_IO / Skywalk-style AWDL TX datapath.

One important safety note from testing: calling active output/flow-control methods on the AWDL virtual interface is unsafe. A previous trace that touched virtual-interface flow-control state caused a kernel panic. Therefore, the latest traces were kept passive and limited to getters such as interface state, pending packet counts, DLT output queue pointers, and DLT12 queue size/capacity.

## Final technical update after the experimental AX210 AWDL investigation

I have now completed a much deeper source- and runtime-grounded investigation of AWDL/AirDrop with Intel AX210 and AirportItlwm under the OCLP-restored Tahoe wireless environment.

This work was performed in a private experimental AirportItlwm branch based on the DexterSLamb fork. It is not part of the official OpenIntelWireless releases, it is not a pull request, and it has not produced a user-ready Kext or reproducible working Intel AirDrop.

The purpose of this update is to correct and substantially refine the technical picture described in the original issue.

POST-PUBLICATION AUDIT NOTE — JULY 2026

A subsequent read-only comparison of official AirportItlwm v2.3.0, the Dexter source baseline, the OCLP-restored Apple environment and Builds 2.3.131–2.3.195 clarified an important methodological distinction. The experimental branch tested a newly constructed explicit Intel AWDL management-plane architecture, not a proved reconstruction of the rare historical one-time-transfer path. The recorded source identities and runtime milestones remain unchanged, but several conclusions have been narrowed.

All preceding-month KGP runtime use and my historical one-time transfer used the official release asset:

AirportItlwm_v2.3.0_stable_Ventura.kext.zip

Dexter commit 51543d6cfecf8aae3f66792b0699f5a1bb16a368 was selected later as the development source baseline. A direct comparison with official OpenIntelWireless v2.3.0 commit 4ac4c79bc7e34f8764038fc382630a29eb46213d found identical Ventura target source, build settings, plist, AWDL/P2P callbacks and generic packet paths. Dexter’s runtime source delta concerns the Sonoma V2 LQM path and is not compiled into the Ventura target. Dexter was therefore not the historical runtime baseline.

1. What OCLP, Apple and AirportItlwm each contribute
The most important conclusion is that these layers must be separated.

OCLP itself is primarily a deployment and compatibility layer, but it materially determines the hybrid Apple runtime. In the later Tahoe environment inspected here, that meant a newer host and some native host components alongside restored Ventura 13.7.2-generation wifip2pd and private frameworks, restored IO80211FamilyLegacy/IOSkywalkFamily components, and a user-selected Ventura-ABI AirportItlwm Kext.

OCLP does not schedule the AX210 radio, create Intel firmware stations or queues, issue Intel Time Events, transmit through an Intel TX queue, or deliver Intel RX packets to awdl0.

The inspected OCLP source does not select or bundle AirportItlwm-Ventura itself. The user’s OpenCore configuration selects the AirportItlwm artifact. OCLP is therefore neither the Intel lower driver nor a completely passive factor with no runtime significance.

Apple supplies most of the AWDL upper plane. The restored Apple environment already contains the virtual-interface model, IO80211AWDLPeerManager, peer lifetime and data-mode machinery, native flow queues, packet preparation, multicast handling, TX status/completion interfaces, RX input interfaces, Finder/AirDrop service logic, and the higher-level IPv6/mDNS behavior that could operate once a usable lower data path exists.

AirportItlwm is the actual Intel hardware driver. For any genuine Intel AWDL path,
AirportItlwm or existing generic Intel mechanisms must ultimately supply the
hardware-specific MAC/PHY/binding/station/queue/Time Event/TX/RX operations required
by Apple’s scheduling, peer, packet and completion contracts.

A Broadcom IOName/device spoof can help select or expose the expected Apple environment, but it does not translate Broadcom commands into Intel commands. AirPortBrcmNIC, Broadcom firmware, DMA/ring handling, IOVARs and Broadcom-private state cannot simply be reused to drive AX210 hardware.

No current evidence indicates that an OCLP source modification is required for the
unresolved Intel lower work. Any future OCLP change would most likely concern
deployment or capability selection rather than replacing the AirportItlwm-side
hardware integration.

2. Important correction to the original awdl0 result
The original issue reported that awdl0 did not exist with the tested Intel configuration.

Official Ventura v2.3.0 did not broadly prove that all AWDL activity was blocked. It returned kIOReturnUnsupported from one exact legacy setVIRTUAL_IF_CREATE() setter path before the older explicit P2P/AWDL allocation body. Official source also had separate visible gaps: requestPacketTx did not perform native virtual-packet dequeue and handoff, raw/action/BPF paths dropped packets, no complete Intel AWDL scheduler was visible, and no visible RX demultiplexer delivered packets to awdl0. These source gaps do not prove that every Apple-superclass, temporary, generic, lifecycle-dependent, binary-specific or alternate-transport runtime path was impossible.

The narrow result of the experimental branch is:

“The KGP branch first enabled and runtime-proved its explicit Ventura setVIRTUAL_IF_CREATE/attach/enable/link-state AWDL VIF path, and later its separate experimental Intel lower-context setup.”

This is not a universal claim that KGP first enabled AWDL. The system now creates an IO80211P2PInterface with the AWDL role, and the controlled Build 2.3.195 runtime showed:

awdl0 present
awdl0 UP
awdl0 RUNNING
link state active
an IPv6 link-local address assigned
This is a real improvement over the original state, but it must not be confused with a usable AWDL data path.

An active awdl0 interface and a link-local IPv6 address prove interface creation and Apple-side lifecycle participation. They do not prove bidirectional L2 packet delivery, mDNS over AWDL, peer-specific data queues, or AirDrop transfer.

3. What the experimental AirportItlwm branch implemented
Across Builds 2.3.131 through 2.3.195, the investigation added or substantially developed the following areas:

These builds chiefly constructed and tested one plausible explicit clean-room Intel AWDL management-plane architecture. After enabling the rejected Ventura VIF path, the branch added its own VIF lifecycle, Intel P2P PHY/MAC/binding, Station 3, TXQ4, scheduling, timing, Time Event and safety architecture. The experiment did not establish that this architecture was the path used by the official release during the historical one-time transfers.

Ventura AWDL VIF creation, attachment, enable/disable and link-state handling
capture of Apple OOB, synchronization, profile, channel-sequence, AF_TX_MODE and requestPacketTx() callbacks
native Apple synchronization-frame template capture and refresh
exact Apple AWDL action-frame classification:
category 0x7f
Apple OUI 00:17:f2
AWDL OUI type 0x08
bounded TLV parsing, including TLV 0x04
peer MAC, channel, frequency, TSF, GP2 and generation tracking
genuine peer and timing-anchor capture
Intel P2P PHY1, P2P Device MAC1 and MAC/PHY binding
channel-6 lower-context configuration
broadcast Station 3
management TXQ4
bounded Session Protection experiments
bounded management-frame submission and matching completion
GP2/host timing correlation
next-AW reservation logic
Intel Time Event request/notification diagnostics
correction of the Intel Time Event response-status predicate
immutable reservation and transaction records
a manually gated Build 2.3.195 safety framework with:
300-second quiet period
privileged one-shot trigger
no automatic retry
no automatic reservation
no automatic Time Event
no automatic TX
safe lower setup
eight immutable transaction slots
bounded explicit STATUS publication
A large part of this source is diagnostic or laboratory control code. It must not be interpreted as production-ready AWDL support.

4. Runtime milestones that were actually reached
Several isolated lower-plane milestones were proven.

Earlier controlled builds showed that:

a bounded P2P Session Protection command could start successfully;
exact Apple AWDL action frames could be received on channel 6;
valid timing information from multiple peers could be recorded;
a management frame could be submitted through Station 3/TXQ4;
the corresponding Intel TX completion could be matched.
Build 2.3.193 reached the most advanced coherent timing boundary. It captured a genuine Apple AWDL peer on channel 6 and decoded:

presence mode 4
AW period 16 TU
63 TU to the next availability window
coherent profile, channel and generation state
approximately 2 microseconds from RX classification to reservation
approximately 63.805 ms of forward command lead
successful reservation creation
successful task staging
entry into the real Time Event worker/command stage
However, Build 2.3.193 did not obtain a valid firmware UID, accept Event Start, or submit TX through that final end-to-end path.

Build 2.3.194 then corrected the host-side response interpretation. The Intel contract requires the documented success bit to be set, no documented error bits, the expected response length, and a nonzero UID. That correction is source- and model-proven, but it remains runtime-unproven.

Important historical exception: isolated one-time send-only AirDrop results
Before this controlled experimental branch was developed, I once completed a real one-time AirDrop transfer from the Hackintosh to a MacBook Pro while using the official stable Ventura release, even though the Hackintosh was not visible as an AirDrop target on the MacBook Pro.

A comparable one-time result was also reported by another user earlier in this issue under the OCLP amfipassbeta environment.

Across the reports presently known to me, only a handful of isolated successes exist, approximately four reports at most. This is an approximate count of presently known reports, not a universal statistic. They occurred under different OCLP codes or variants, none has become a reliable procedure, and no synchronized successful runtime capture exists.

These observations must not be ignored: they prevent a categorical claim that an outbound official-AirportItlwm transfer never occurred or was absolutely impossible. However:

the result was not reproducible;
the exact mechanism and transport path were not identified;
the Hackintosh still lacked normal reverse discovery/visibility;
no stable bidirectional AWDL operation was established;
and the controlled Builds 2.3.193–2.3.195 did not reproduce that success.
Their rarity and missing evidence make them unsuitable as a reproducible experimental or development baseline. Even many failed attempts would establish only exceptional rarity under the tested conditions, not falsify the historical observations.

No single transport hypothesis currently dominates. The strongest broad family may combine restored Apple peer/flow/runtime behavior, generic AirportItlwm lower resources, temporary or lifecycle-dependent state, possible genuine peer-to-peer use of generic lower mechanisms, or another Apple-controlled transport decision. Pure infrastructure remains possible, but no route, socket or packet evidence justifies ranking it first.

The correct conclusion is therefore not that any Intel AirDrop transfer is fundamentally impossible. It is that current AirportItlwm does not provide a complete, understood, reliable or reproducible AWDL/AirDrop implementation, and the mechanism of the isolated official-release successes remains unknown.

5. Final Build 2.3.195 result
The final controlled Build 2.3.195 experiment successfully:

completed the 300-second quiet period;
reached READY-FOR-MANUAL-TRIGGER;
accepted exactly one privileged trigger;
entered LOWER-SETUP-IN-PROGRESS;
created PHY1, MAC1, Binding1, Station 3 and TXQ4;
completed the lower-context predicate with stable generation;
entered ARMED-WAITING-FOR-POST-TRIGGER-PEER;
preserved ordinary Wi-Fi and Bluetooth operation;
suppressed all automatic background attempts;
consumed no transaction slot before a real command.
It then ended with:

POST-TRIGGER-PEER-TIMEOUT

No new exact Apple AWDL action frame reached the RX classifier during the fresh three-second post-setup peer window.

The attempt therefore stopped before reservation and before the real Time Event helper. It did not test:

the corrected Time Event response parser;
a valid firmware UID;
Event Start;
management TX;
TX completion;
remote visibility.
Accordingly, Build 2.3.195 must not be described as a Time Event, firmware-command, Station 3, TXQ4, TX or completion failure.

The cross-stack scheduling analysis found that Build 2.3.195 had configured and bound the channel-6 lower context but had deliberately suppressed the earlier Session Protection producer. A configured PHY/MAC/binding does not itself guarantee that the shared radio leaves the infrastructure channel and occupies channel 6 during the receive window.

No active channel-6 scheduler grant or physical channel-6 dwell was proved during that three-second window. POST-TRIGGER-PEER-TIMEOUT therefore constrains only this exact manual KGP sequence. Station 3 and TXQ4 were plausible and experimentally validated lower resources used by the clean-room architecture; they were not proved universal requirements. The fresh-peer timing anchor was likewise a conservative KGP policy, not a proved prerequisite for every possible outbound transfer or the historical events.

6. What remains unresolved for a reliable implementation
The controlled experiments establish which stages were not reached by the
final experimental branch. They do not prove that every lower component listed
below is entirely absent from every possible AirportItlwm/OCLP runtime path.

The isolated historical transfers prevent a categorical impossibility claim, but
they do not identify a reproducible Apple/Intel path. Their exact mechanisms were
not captured, and the controlled experimental branch did not prove equivalence to
them.

The following gaps are directly demonstrated by the controlled tests:

no reliable and reproducible Intel AWDL scheduling policy;
no completed corrected Time Event, nonzero UID and Event Start transaction;
no reproducible management-advertisement sequence;
no reliable remote visibility of the Hackintosh;
no reproducible one-way or bidirectional AirDrop transfer;
no validated reset, sleep/wake and long-duration AWDL stability.
The following source areas appear incomplete, disconnected or insufficiently
understood for a controlled production implementation:

Apple peer-manager lifecycle and data-mode integration;
peer-specific Intel station, queue and TID handling;
native Apple packet dequeue, ownership and completion reporting;
RX peer/context demultiplexing and delivery to awdl0;
packet_info_tag and IO80211P2PInterface input requirements;
reliable AWDL IPv6 and mDNS transport.
These items describe the most plausible areas in which a clean, reproducible
implementation may require further work. The one-time transfer results mean
that it cannot currently be claimed that every item is wholly absent or that
all of them must necessarily be implemented from scratch before any transfer
can occur.

Several overlapping possibilities remain open: Apple-owned peer/flow behavior
interacting with generic AirportItlwm resources and temporary or lifecycle-dependent
state; genuine peer-to-peer behavior through generic lower mechanisms; another
Apple-controlled transport decision; or a more explicit Apple-to-Intel bridge. The
evidence does not rank one mechanism first.

7. Development scope and uncertaintyNo credible completion schedule can currently be provided.

A clean and explicit reproducible implementation would span several independent
layers: reliable Intel channel scheduling, management advertisements and remote
visibility, Apple peer lifecycle, peer-specific Intel stations and queues, native
packet ownership and completion reporting, RX delivery to awdl0, IPv6 and mDNS,
and reset, sleep/wake and long-term stability—or functional equivalents supplied
through other validated mechanisms.

The isolated one-time send-only AirDrop results prevent categorical impossibility
claims but are too rare and poorly captured to establish a reusable partial path.
No single mechanism currently dominates, and it cannot be assumed that the answer is
either simply stabilizing an existing path or implementing every listed component
from scratch.
Even the smallest controlled next experiment would test only one prerequisite
and would not produce AirDrop by itself. Reliable remote discovery would
require several additional scheduling and management stages, while stable
bidirectional transfer would additionally require the complete peer lifecycle,
station and queue management, packet ownership, completion reporting, RX
delivery, IPv6, mDNS, reset and sleep/wake paths.

Accordingly, the controlled evidence does not support treating reproducible Intel
AirDrop as a one-day fix. Depending on which mechanism or combination of mechanisms
proves relevant, future work could range from a small number of focused investigations
to a long-term driver-development and reverse-engineering project. A defensible
completion date cannot currently be given.

8. Current practical conclusion
This investigation does not show that Intel AWDL is impossible.

The handful of isolated official-release transfers, including my own and the comparable report in this issue, prevents a categorical claim that outbound Intel AirDrop never occurred. Their mechanism remains unknown, and they do not provide a controlled, understood, reliable or reproducible path.

The controlled evidence does not support treating complete, reproducible Intel
AirDrop as one missing callback or a small compatibility patch.

A clean, understood, reliable and maintainable implementation may require substantial
driver-development work involving:

Intel multi-context scheduling;
Apple private driver contracts;
peer lifecycle;
firmware station/queue management;
packet ownership;
RX and TX completion semantics;
power/reset stability;
ongoing maintenance across macOS releases.
Even the first remote-visibility milestone is not yet guaranteed. A stable bidirectional data plane may require several additional and mutually dependent development layers, functional equivalents supplied through existing Apple/generic mechanisms, or some combination, followed by substantial stability and maintenance work.

For that reason, I am ending the current active experimental development phase at Build 2.3.195 and freezing it as a research and evidence milestone.

No further active AWDL architecture build is planned without new concrete technical evidence, a developer explanation, or a newly identified bounded boundary.

No experimental Kext is being released, and none of this work should be treated as a replacement for the official AirportItlwm releases.

9. Practical next step
The practical investigation no longer depends on reproducing another extraordinarily rare success.

First, compare the presently known isolated reports for common facts such as exact artifact, hardware, macOS/OCLP variant, direction, visibility, infrastructure and Bluetooth state, and preceding lifecycle transitions.

Second, use a verified unmodified official v2.3.0 Ventura artifact in one fully documented current OCLP environment to characterize what reproducibly happens during an ordinary failed AirDrop attempt: interface/object state, counters, routes, neighbors, process sockets, bounded Apple-service logs, primary-interface traffic and relevant Wi-Fi/Bluetooth/service transitions. This characterizes the normal current official failure path; it does not reproduce or falsify the historical one-time mechanism.

Third, add minimal passive instrumentation based directly on official 4ac4c79 only if that characterization exposes one concrete unresolved callback or ownership boundary. A successful transfer is not a prerequisite. Historical OCLP reconstruction may continue as archival research but should not be treated as likely to reproduce a success.

I don't think AWDL has ever worked.
The awdl0 interface is present up to Monterey, but AirDrop doesn't work (at least not with my AX201). When you select "Share via AirDrop," you can see IPv6 packets being sent out over the awdl0 interface (Wireshark), but no packets are received.
With a native AirPort module, you see traffic in both directions after selecting "Share via AirDrop", regardless of which side initiates the sharing.
I conclude from this that the awdl0 interface (where present) doesn't really work with Intel cards—or rather, it isn't connected to the network.

In Sonoma, there is no `awdl0` interface either, yet AirDrop transmissions are still possible (albeit only outgoing). In this scenario, QUIC packets are transmitted via the `wlan0` interface—and it even works when the recipient is connected only via LAN.
However, the recipient must be on an reachable network, a requirement that does not apply to native AirDrop (which connects ad-hoc via AWDL).

I suspect that the AirDrop feature "Continue transfer over the Internet" is the reason why AirDrop works on Intel cards at all—albeit with limitations. This feature was introduced with iOS 17 / macOS Sonoma. Pure—or perhaps more accurately, native—AirDrop (via the ad-hoc connection) does not appear to be possible with Intel cards.
